extracted.intended_audience: writers submitting short fiction (magazines, journals, literary publications)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical editorial guidance for writers preparing short stories for magazine/journal submissions, focused on getting work out of the slush pile and noticed by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-winded openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings that spend many words on exposition, backstory, or scene-setting and hide the story’s main action or 'meat' (e.g., 500 words of setup in a 5,000-word story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the scene you’re building toward and weave world/plot/character details into action as it unfolds. Identify what happens between the first paragraph and the first crucial scene; if it’s mostly exposition, trim. If you prefer longer openings, focus descriptive writing on a moment important to the character and have characters interact with the setting (example: move a character through a marketplace while revealing history). Pair story action with description rather than dumping backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disconnected endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Endings that fail to follow through on promises or elements introduced earlier, or which simply string together 'cool' moments that don’t connect to the plot or characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight every time you give the reader chunks of character, world, or story information and check whether those elements resurface or affect the ending. Ensure twists are unexpected but consistent with the story’s internal logic and characters. If using coincidence or ambiguous/odd endings, provide a thread the reader can hold onto (unique descriptions, a strong character or narrative voice) so the ending impacts the reader and feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of emotional beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that focus on idea or events at the expense of how those events affect characters and readers — failing to create a feeling or reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what you want characters to feel at key moments and what reaction you want from readers; then rewrite scenes to evoke those feelings via subtext rather than direct statement. Use figurative language, metaphor, simile, and sensory detail to capture moments. Find a middle ground between showing and telling. Even low-emotion pieces must cause some reaction in readers; pinpoint the reactions and actively create them on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclear main character(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories without a clear, active main character — protagonists who are passive 'windows' into events rather than participants who experience or drive change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which character the story should follow and introduce that character (ideally on the first page). Make the main character an active participant through action, characterization, or emotional response so readers understand the stakes and weight of events. If you want an unreliable or blurred perspective, still show who that person is and how they fit into the world (second-person POV can blur reader/character but must still be anchored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong story for a market
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting work that doesn’t fit a publication’s editorial lean, genre focus, or audience expectations — often resulting from not reading the magazine or misunderstanding its current preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the magazines you submit to and learn their editorial lean, subject matter, and voice. Know genre and form distinctions (literary vs. genre, flash vs. short fiction, hybrid). Don’t treat submissions as a numbers game without regard to fit; aligning your story with a market increases chances. If you don’t want to tailor to markets, consider self-publishing or venues with lower admission hurdles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cliché or overdone topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Using worn tropes or themes without offering a fresh perspective or new contribution (writing outdated or commonly repeated story types without a twist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read recent work in target publications to learn which topics are overused. Identify the conventions/tropes you’re using and ask what you’re doing differently — remix, reinvent, or find a new angle. If your story offers nothing new, write a different story or reshape your approach so genre conventions are used in intelligent and surprising ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing happens (lack of change or charge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that merely describe a world or moment without change, conflict, or an offering of new insight — resulting in no driving force to engage readers or editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the story takes readers on a journey that produces change or fresh insight for characters, the world, or the reader (this can be subtle). Determine what you are offering the reader in exchange for their time and make that experience clear on the page. If your piece is intentionally low on conflict, clarify its purpose (e.g., presenting an experience or atmosphere) and show how it yields something memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the story rise to the top / resonate with editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond technical craft, a submission must 'touch' an editor — resonate, feel distinct, and stand out among many well-crafted pieces in the queue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish elements (opening, ending, emotional beats, character clarity, market fit, originality, narrative charge) so the story registers with an editor. Recognize that every other submission is a 'unique snowflake,' and focus on ways your story can create an emotional or intellectual hook. Iteration, learning from rejections, and targeted submission strategies (knowing markets, revising weak elements) help move a story out of the queue.
